## Hosea 12 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: *“Ephraim chases the wind and pursues the east wind all day long; he multiplies lies and violence; he makes a covenant with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt.”*

- **“Feeds on wind” / “chases the wind”** — The imagery pictures futility and emptiness. Ephraim’s idols and foreign alliances are like trying to eat air; they provide no real nourishment. The Hebrew verb for “feeds” (*ra‘ah*) means to graze or pasture, picturing livestock grazing on nothing. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/)

- **“East wind”** — The sirocco, the hot, parching desert wind from the Arabian steppe that scorches crops and dries springs. It combines the notions of emptiness *and* destructiveness. Ephraim is not merely grazing on wind but chasing the very thing that will kill him. Wetzstein is quoted by Ellicott: “This wind is more frequent in winter and early spring, when, if it continues long, the tender vegetation is parched up… Both man and beast feel sickly while it prevails.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

- **“Lies and violence”** — The lies are diplomatic treacheries: Ephraim signs covenants and breaks them. Violence (*shod*) can mean both the violence they inflict and the devastation they will receive. Gill notes that idolatry is at root a lie, and multiplying idols only increases their desolation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

- **Covenant with Assyria / oil to Egypt** — Israel played “both ends against the middle,” making treaties with one superpower while sending tribute to the other. 2 Kings 17:4 records Hoshea swearing loyalty to Assyria while secretly sending messengers to Egypt. The Pulpit Commentary explains that oil was sent as a present, not trade — Israel was rich in olive oil (Deut 8:8), and Egypt lacked it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hosea/12.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

---

### v. 2: *“The LORD also brings a charge against Judah. He will punish Jacob according to his ways and repay him according to his deeds.”*

- **“Charge” / “controversy”** — The Hebrew *rib* is a legal term for a covenant lawsuit. God acts as both plaintiff and judge. This is the same word used in Hosea 4:1 (“the LORD has a case against the inhabitants of the land”). Now Judah is also indicted, not just the northern kingdom. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary; https://bible.org/seriespage/hosea-12)

- **“Jacob”** — Ellicott takes “Jacob” here to refer to the northern kingdom specifically, contrasting with Judah. Others (e.g., Constable) see “Jacob” as encompassing both kingdoms since both descended from him. The principle laid down is divine retribution: God repays each according to his deeds (cf. Gal 6:7). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-12.html)

- **Gill** adds that God “visits” — which can be in mercy or judgment depending on the ways being visited. Here the ways are crooked, so God visits in punishment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 3: *“In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God.”*

- **“He grasped his brother’s heel”** — This refers to Jacob’s birth (Gen 25:26). Hosea sees in this prenatal act the defining trait of Jacob’s character: a “heel-catcher,” a supplanter, a deceiver. Boice is quoted: “To grasp the heel also meant to go behind one’s back in order to deceive or trick him.” The prophet’s point: modern Israel shares the same crooked character as their forefather. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

- **“In his vigor he wrestled with God”** — The Hebrew *sarah* means to strive, persist in struggle, or contend. It is the same verb used in Gen 32:28 where Jacob is renamed Israel (“you have striven with God”). While some see the heel-grasping as an accusation, the wrestling with God is generally viewed positively — a persevering, tenacious faith. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

- **Gill** elaborates that this wrestling was not merely natural strength but strength given by God. Jacob prevailed “by his strength” — not his own natural strength but the strength of faith in prayer that God supplied. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 4: *“Yes, he struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor; he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there—”*

- **“He struggled with the angel and prevailed”** — The “angel” is the Angel of the LORD, understood in conservative Protestant tradition as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (theophany). Gill argues this was no created angel but the uncreated Son of God, citing Gen 48:16, Isa 63:9, and Mal 3:1. He “prevailed” not by overpowering God but by surrendering and clinging in desperation. Guzik: “We prevail when we lose and know it, surrendering to God.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/)

- **“He wept and sought His favor”** — This detail is not in Genesis 32 but is supplied by prophetic inspiration. Jacob wept not from the pain of his dislocated hip but in desperate supplication for blessing. The tears were “for the blessing he sought,” an expression of humble, ardent, importunate prayer. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/)

- **“He found Him at Bethel”** — Bethel was the place where God first appeared to Jacob in the dream of the ladder (Gen 28) and again when Jacob returned and built an altar (Gen 35). Gill points out the tragic irony: the northern kingdom had turned Bethel (“house of God”) into Beth-aven (“house of idolatry/iniquity”) by placing a golden calf there. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

- **“There He spoke with us”** — Gill explains that God spoke “with us” (all Israel) because the nation was in Jacob’s loins at that time; the promises given at Bethel concerned the multiplication of Jacob’s descendants and the gift of Canaan. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

- **Ellicott** notes that “at Bethel He found him” refers not to a single occasion but repeated encounters: Gen 28 and Gen 35, and in the subsequent history of Israel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 5: *“—the LORD is the God of Hosts—the LORD is His name of renown.”*

- This verse identifies the One with whom Jacob wrestled: He is **YHWH**, the God of Hosts. “God of Hosts” (*Yahweh Tseva’ot*) refers to His command over the angelic armies and all created hosts. Ellicott identifies the “hosts” as the stars conceived as celestial spirits around God’s throne (1 Kings 22:19; Job 1:6; Ps 103:21). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

- **“His memorial” / “His name of renown”** — Jehovah is the name by which God is remembered across all generations. It expresses His self-existence, eternity, and immutability. The same God Jacob met is available to his descendants. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 6: *“But you must return to your God, maintaining love and justice, and always waiting on your God.”*

- **“Return”** — The Hebrew *shub* is a Qal Imperfect used as a Jussive (a command). It is the classic prophetic call to repentance. The ESV renders it “So you, by the help of your God, return,” emphasizing that even repentance requires divine assistance. Guzik: “We can never even return to the LORD without His help.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

- **“Maintaining love and justice”** — Hebrew *chesed* (covenant loyalty, mercy, steadfast love) and *mishpat* (justice, right judgment). These are the weightier matters of the covenant (Matt 23:23). They echo Hosea 2:19; 4:1; 6:6; 10:12. Constable: “They should practice loyal love and justice in dealing with one another rather than being like the old Jacob.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-12.html)

- **“Always waiting on your God”** — This is not passive idleness but active, continual trust and hope in God. Gill links it to waiting for the Messiah and salvation (cf. Gen 49:18). The Targum paraphrases: “wait for the redemption or salvation of thy God continually.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

- **Ellicott** adds that this verse contains an implied contrast between the patriarch who sought God and his degenerate descendants in Hosea’s day. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 7: *“A merchant loves to defraud with dishonest scales in his hands.”*

- **“A merchant” / “Canaan”** — The Hebrew word *kena‘an* can mean both “Canaanite” and “merchant,” since the Canaanites (especially the Phoenicians) were known as traders. Hosea is calling Ephraim a “Canaanite” — not ethnically but morally. As Ellicott puts it: “Ephraim had imbibed Phoenicia’s love of gain and habits of unscrupulous trade.” Guzik quotes Clarke: “Ephraim is as corrupt as those heathenish traffickers were.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/)

- **“Dishonest scales”** — False balances were an abomination to the LORD (Prov 11:1; 20:23). Merchants would carry two sets of weights — heavier for buying, lighter for selling. The phrase “loves to oppress” indicates this was not occasional but a settled disposition. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 8: *“And Ephraim boasts: ‘How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself. In all my labors, they can find in me no iniquity that is sinful.’”*

- **Self-deception about wealth** — Ephraim equated prosperity with divine approval. They credited their riches to their own labor and denied any wrongdoing. Gill notes they “did not acknowledge that their riches, and power to get them, were of God.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/12.htm)

- **“No iniquity that is sinful”** — This boast claims that even a thorough audit would find nothing seriously wrong — perhaps minor errors but nothing deserving the name “sin.” Guzik compares this to the Laodicean church in Revelation 3 that said “I am rich… and have need of nothing” while being spiritually wretched. Ellicott also draws this parallel to the Laodicean church. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 9: *“But I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt. I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast.”*

- **“I am the LORD your God ever since… Egypt”** — This is the full covenant formula (cf. Exod 20:2). God asserts that He has been their God from the beginning of their national existence. His claim on them precedes and overrides all their wealth. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary)

- **“Dwell in tents”** — Two interpretations exist among the commentators: (1) A positive recollection of the wilderness ideal, when Israel depended wholly on God (cf. Hos 2:14; 9:10; 11:1-4). (2) A threat of judgment — God will reduce them from fine houses to makeshift tents, just as during the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) but permanently. The immediate context (v. 8) strongly favors the second option. The Pulpit Commentary calls it a threat of “expulsion, desolation, and despair” to the worldly-minded. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-12-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 10: *“I spoke through the prophets and multiplied their visions; I gave parables through the prophets.”*

- **God’s abundant revelation** — The people had no excuse. God spoke “at sundry times and in divers manners” (Heb 1:1). The three terms — spoken, multiplied visions, gave parables/similitudes — cover the full range of prophetic communication. Constable: “Nevertheless in spite of so many exhortations to return to the Lord the people had not responded.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-12.html)

- **Spurgeon’s sermon on this verse** (July 25, 1858) develops the theme that God preaches “by similitudes” every day through providence. He notes how Hosea himself became a living parable by marrying Gomer, and how God uses everyday life to speak to human consciences. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/hosea-12.html)

---

### v. 11: *“Is there iniquity in Gilead? They will surely come to nothing. Do they sacrifice bulls in Gilgal? Indeed, their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field.”*

- **Gilead** — A region east of the Jordan known for idolatry. The rhetorical question implies an obvious “yes,” and the judgment is that they are “worthless” or “come to nothing.” Ellicott suggests this refers to the desolating invasion of Gilead by Tiglath-pileser III in 734 BC (2 Kings 15:29). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

- **Gilgal** — A major worship center. The Hebrew involves a wordplay: *Gilgal* sounds like *gallim* (“heaps of stones”). The sacred site will become rubble in plowed fields. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the pagan altars “were built high and stately to add dignity to the pagan god” but will be brought low. Guzik: “the only altars will be the hills made by the furrows of the field.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 12: *“Jacob fled to the land of Aram and Israel worked for a wife—for a wife he tended sheep.”*

- **Jacob’s humble origins** — The prophet reminds Israel of their patriarch’s low estate: a refugee fleeing Esau (Gen 27:43), working as a shepherd for Laban to pay for his wives (Gen 29). Constable points out that this recalls the nation’s humble beginnings and God’s providential care. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-12.html)

- The sequence contrasts Jacob’s humility with Ephraim’s arrogant prosperity. Jacob fled to Aram; now Ephraim courts Aram (Assyria/Syria) for political gain — but instead of humble service, they do it with lies and double-dealing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/)

---

### v. 13: *“But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved.”*

- **“A prophet” = Moses** — All commentators agree Moses is meant (cf. Deut 18:18; 34:10-12). The point: it was not political alliances or human cleverness that saved Israel, but God working through His prophetic word. Constable notes the implied warning: “they should not, therefore, have despised the prophets that Yahweh had sent them since Moses (cf. v.10).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-12.html)

- Ellicott adds a hopeful note: “there is, perhaps, a hint that the Lord would yet again save Israel from worse than Egyptian bondage by the words and warnings of a prophet.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

---

### v. 14: *“Ephraim has provoked bitter anger, so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him and repay him for his contempt.”*

- **“Provoked bitter anger”** — The language is strong and personal. Ellicott reads it as “Ephraim hath provoked bitter feeling.” The offense is not merely rule-breaking but a personal affront to the covenant Lord. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/12.htm)

- **“Leave his bloodguilt upon him”** — God will not remove or forgive the guilt of their bloodshed (possibly including child sacrifice to Molech, as Ellicott suggests). Constable: “He would not remove the guilt of their sins by forgiving them but would pay them back with punishment and shame.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-12.html)

- **“Repay him for his contempt”** — The word “reproach” returns upon Ephraim’s own head. The closing note of the chapter is severe judgment, underlining that despite the call to repentance (v. 6), Ephraim’s persistent rebellion will bring inevitable consequences. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-12/)

---

## Denominational Differences & Other Views

**What could not be retrieved:** Because search and fetch tool limits were reached, I was unable to access dedicated pages from the following requested sources:
- **Reformed:** Ligonier, Monergism, The Gospel Coalition — though the Precept Austin and Enduring Word commentaries draw heavily on Reformed teachers (Boice, etc.)
- **Baptist:** DesiringGod.org, GTY.org
- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** Wesley.nnu.edu, Seedbed.com
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic:** PneumaReview.com, SamStorms.org, AG.org
- **Lutheran:** LCMS.org, 1517.org
- **Catholic/Orthodox:** NewAdvent.org, Catholic.com, OCA.org
- **Modern scholarship:** BibleOdyssey.org, NETBible.org notes

**Brief note on the Chadash/Angel debate (v. 4):** One area where traditions may differ is the identity of the “angel” with whom Jacob wrestled. The traditional conservative Protestant reading (Gill, Guzik, Precept Austin) identifies the angel as a pre-incarnate Christ/theophany. Catholic and Orthodox traditions also read this as a theophany, though Eastern Orthodox hymnography sometimes identifies the angel as the “Angel of Great Counsel” (Christ). Modern critical scholarship (not accessed) might treat the Genesis account as an older folkloric story about a night demon or river spirit that was later theologized. I was unable to verify these readings from the designated sites.

**On v. 6 (“return… wait on your God”)**: Hyper-grace or prosperity teachers might contest the idea that repentance and “maintaining love and justice” are required of God’s people, potentially treating this passage as old-covenant language. I could not locate specific prosperity/hyper-grace treatments of this chapter from the allowed sites.

---

*Summary:* The traditional reading across the commentaries accessed (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Guzik, Constable, Precept Austin) is remarkably unified on this chapter: Hosea 12 indicts Ephraim/Israel for deceit and covenant-breaking, uses the patriarch Jacob as both a mirror of Israel’s crookedness and a model of repentant clinging to God, warns against trusting wealth and foreign alliances, and calls the nation to return to YHWH with covenant faithfulness. Interpretive differences are minor (e.g., whether v. 9 is positive or negative, whether “Jacob” in v. 2 means the North or both kingdoms). Fuller denominational contrasts would require additional searching.
